facts.text: On this date in 1980, Iraq invaded Iran, beginning a war that lasted eight years, killed over a million people, and ended with no territory gained by either side.

On this date in 1792, France abolished the monarchy and declared itself a republic — a decision made the day after its first military victory at Valmy convinced revolutionaries the new order could survive.
Mongolia has more horses than people: roughly 4.3 million horses for 3.4 million humans, and about a third of the population still lives nomadically, moving with their herds across the steppe.

The city of Jakarta is sinking so fast — up to 25 centimeters per year in some districts — that Indonesia has already begun moving its capital to Nusantara, a new city being carved from Borneo's jungle.
France is the most visited country on Earth, drawing over 100 million tourists a year to a population of 68 million — meaning tourists outnumber residents by nearly 50 percent every year.

On this day in 1998, the Federal Reserve orchestrated a $3.6 billion bailout of Long-Term Capital Management — a hedge fund run by two Nobel laureates whose models had spectacularly failed to predict Russia's debt default.

On this day in 1869, financiers Jay Gould and James Fisk attempted to corner the entire U.S. gold market, triggering Black Friday and wiping out thousands of traders before President Grant ordered emergency gold sales.
The New York Stock Exchange was founded under a buttonwood tree in 1792 by 24 brokers — the agreement they signed was named after that tree and fit on a single sheet of paper.
Berkshire Hathaway's original business was textiles. Warren Buffett later called buying it the worst trade of his life, estimating the mistake cost him $200 billion in compounded opportunity.
The entire market cap of the Dutch East India Company at its 1637 peak, adjusted for today's money, exceeded $8 trillion — larger than Apple, Microsoft, and Saudi Aramco combined.
On this day in 1791, Michael Faraday was born — the man who discovered electromagnetic induction with no formal math training, essentially inventing the electric age by intuition alone.
On September 22, 1956, the first commercial nuclear power station began feeding electricity to the UK grid, making atomic fire a household utility.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its matter would weigh roughly a billion tons on Earth.
Your body replaces about 3.8 million cells per second. The person reading this sentence is measurably different from the one who started it.
Octopuses have three hearts, blue copper-based blood, and neurons distributed throughout their arms — each limb thinks semi-independently of the brain.
On this day in 1862, Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation — a document older than the unification of Italy, Canada as a nation, and the invention of the telephone.
Oxford University was already 300 years old when the Aztec Empire was founded. Some institutions outlast entire civilizations.
On this day in 1776, Nathan Hale was executed by the British. He was 21. The country he died for was 73 days old.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. Ancient Egypt was ancient even to ancient Egyptians.
The fax machine was invented in 1843 — before the American Civil War, before the transcontinental railroad, and 33 years before Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone.
Meraki (μεράκι): Greek for doing something with soul, creativity, or love — leaving a piece of yourself in your work. It has no single-word English equivalent.
Sonder: the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined in 2012 by John Koenig for his Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows.
Vellichor: the strange wistfulness of used bookshops. Also coined by Koenig — proof that naming a feeling can make it bearable.
On this day in 1791, Michael Faraday was born. The word 'ion' — from the Greek ienai, 'to go' — was coined in his correspondence with William Whewell in 1834.
Hiraeth: a Welsh longing for a home that may never have existed. It folds homesickness, grief, and nostalgia into a single untranslatable ache.
On this date in 2017, China's ban on ICOs triggered a 40% drop in Bitcoin's price within two weeks — then Bitcoin went on to hit $20,000 by December, making the panic sellers the story's losers.
On this date in 2021, the SEC formally rejected VanEck's Bitcoin ETF application, citing manipulation concerns — the same regulator approved a spot Bitcoin ETF just 28 months later.
Ethereum's gas limit is not set by protocol decree — miners (now validators) vote it up or down each block, making throughput a rolling negotiation rather than a fixed rule.

The Bitcoin genesis block contains the headline 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' — not as metadata, but embedded directly in the coinbase transaction, making it immutable on-chain forever.
Satoshi Nakamoto's unmoved wallet addresses hold roughly 1.1 million BTC, meaning the protocol's anonymous founder controls a larger position than any known institutional holder on earth.
On this date in 2017, DeepMind's AlphaGo team published the AlphaGo Zero paper — a system that learned Go from zero human data, surpassing all prior versions in 40 days of self-play.
On this date in 2009, ImageNet launched publicly, seeding the dataset that would trigger the 2012 deep learning inflection point three years later.
GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed roughly 50 GWh of electricity — comparable to the annual consumption of 4,500 average US households.
The first neural network to beat humans at a video game, Atari Breakout, was DQN in 2013. It discovered the tunnel strategy — exploiting a corner bounce — that human experts had used for decades.
Transformer attention scales as O(n²) in sequence length, which is why a model reading 1M tokens costs roughly 1,000× more compute per layer than one reading 1K tokens.
